title: Hypothermia: what to do
asks: how do i warm up someone with hypothermia
he fell in the creek and is freezing what do i do
should i give hot drinks for hypothermia
what to do when someone stops shivering
hypothermia no pulse do i do cpr
partner wet and cold, shivering hard, how do we warm him, over
answer: Hypothermia is a true medical emergency and requires evacuation. Seek medical aid.
Stop further heat loss: get the person out of the cold and into shelter.
Replace all wet clothing with dry clothing or other insulation.
Insulate the person from the ground with foam pads, branches or leaves, so they are not lying directly on it.
Wrap the person from head to toe in sleeping bags, blankets, plastic, bubble wrap or newspapers. Leave the face uncovered.
Only if the person is fully alert and able to swallow: slowly give warm, sweet drinks or sugary food. The sugar gives energy for shivering.
If the person is responsive and shivering: shivering rewarms the body effectively once heat loss has been reduced.
Handle the person gently, keep them lying flat and avoid unnecessary movement.
If the person is hypothermic and not shivering, evacuate immediately.

Sources differ on adding heat (hot water bottles, heating pads, warmed blankets). The Army cold-injury bulletin says to apply external heat only to people who have stopped shivering (or whose injury or poisoning is making them lose heat faster). The HHS ship's medical manual says external heat should be used for people who are not shivering, have a reduced level of consciousness or are unconscious. The Army first aid manual says rewarming a severely hypothermic person should be done by medical professionals; while waiting for help, focus on preventing further heat loss.

If the person is unresponsive: look for breathing and a pulse for at least 1 minute before starting CPR. Breathing may be as slow as 3-4 breaths per minute and the pulse as slow as 10-15 beats per minute.
If no pulse is detected, start chest compressions and evacuate.
Evacuate as soon as possible, with the person lying down.
warnings: Give no food or drink to a person who is not shivering, is drowsy or confused, or is unconscious: they can inhale it.
HHS: do not put a person who is not shivering or not fully conscious in a hot shower or hot bath, and do not let them sit, stand or exercise.
Do not allow tobacco, alcohol or caffeinated drinks.
Never put a heat source directly on the skin: cold skin is easily burned.
Check for a pulse before CPR: chest compressions on a hypothermic person who still has a pulse could trigger a dangerous heart rhythm.
No one should be pronounced dead until they have been rewarmed.

quotes.text: The goals of field management of hypothermia are to rescue, examine, insulate, and rapidly transport. Hypothermia is a true medical emergency and requires evacuation.

The goals for first aid for hypothermia are to rescue, examine, insulate, and rapidly transport. If untreated, hypothermia is a true medical emergency and requires evacuation. Evacuate as soon as possible with the casualty lying down.

The immediate goal during field treatment is to limit further heat loss. All wet clothing should be replaced with dry clothing/other insulation systems/materials and the patient moved to a sheltered area. Patients can be wrapped in sleeping bags, bubble wrap, plastic, blankets, and newspapers. If minimal shelter is available, insulation from the ground is especially important with foam pads, branches, and leaves used to insulate the patient so he or she is not lying directly on the ground. For responsive patients, shivering (endogenous rewarming) is effective once heat loss has been reduced. Warm, sugary drinks should be given with supervision.

Re-warming techniques include— • Remove the casualty from the cold environment. • Replace wet clothing with dry clothing. • Cover the casualty with insulating material or blanket. • Wrap the casualty from head to toe. • Avoid unnecessary movement from the casualty. • If the casualty is conscious, slowly give high caloric sweet warm fluids. • Seek medical aid.
When using a blanket or any passive heating material, it is crucial to wrap the casualty completely, including their head, but ensure the face remains uncovered to prevent breathing obstructions.

For mild hypothermia, (e.g., the patient is alert and vigorously shivering), remove the wet clothing, provide a barrier to evaporation, and insulate the patient from further heat loss (including the head and neck). For patients who are fully conscious and who can eat or drink, supplying sugar containing food or drinks is appropriate, in order to provide energy for the patient’s shivering. Warm fluids may also be provided.
Early intervention is imperative to take advantage of the heat generated from shivering. Remove wet clothing and increase dry insulation.
Environmental hypothermic casualties should be monitored and gently handled as afterdrop is not always observed.
Provide warm food or fluid to conscious Soldiers. Soldiers who are hypothermic and not shivering must be immediately evacuated.

Active external rewarming techniques (for example, radiant heat, hot water bottles, electric blankets, forced hot air, warm water immersion) should be applied only to individuals who have ceased shivering or have a traumatic or toxicological vasodilation that exacerbates the rate of heat loss, since increasing skin temperature will blunt shivering and reduce the rate of rewarming.

For moderate or severe hypothermia (e.g., the patient is not shivering, has a reduced level of consciousness or is unconscious), maintain the patient in a horizontal posture. Do not permit them to sit, stand or exercise, and do not put them in a hot shower or hot bath. If available, administer heated, humidified oxygen. Insulate them as above, but do not provide any food or fluids by mouth. Moderate or severely hypothermia victims have both a reduced gag reflex and a diminished cough reflex, thus increasing their risk for aspiration (inhaling) fluid or food particles. External sources of heat should be used to rewarm the patient (e.g., forced heated air, heating pads, hot water bottles, warmed blankets, radiant heat, body-to-body rewarming, etc.). However, be aware that cold skin is easily burned (severe burns have resulted from hot water bottles placed directly on hypothermic skin), so insulate the skin from direct contact to warm objects.

If no low reading thermometer is available, it is wise to consider the patient to be in severe hypothermia if the following signs and symptoms are present: • no shivering in spite of being very cold • mental changes such as drowsiness, confusion or unconsciousness • abnormal coordination, trouble walking or using the hands, and difficulty talking.

Attempting to rewarm a severely hypothermic person should be done by medical professionals using appropriate techniques. While waiting for help to arrive, focus on preventing further heat loss and providing support to the person.

Signs of breathing or cardiac activity (and/or respiratory and pulse rate) should be sought for at least 1 minute because respiratory rates may be as low as 3-4 breaths per minute, pulse rates as low as 10-15 beats per minute, and pulse volume low and breaths shallow.

In unresponsive patients, it is essential to assess peripheral pulses. Although these pulses are very difficult to detect, they must be determined before cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) is initiated. Even slow heart rates may provide enough blood for the low metabolic demand of the patient. If CPR is initiated in a hypothermic person with a pulse, chest compressions could convert sinus bradycardia into a ventricular arrhythmia.
Do not begin chest compressions if the patient has any heart beat or pulse, even if it is very slow. This could cause dangerous abnormal heart rhythms and further complications.
If no pulse is detected, chest compressions will be initiated and the casualty evacuated.
Do not allow the casualty to use tobacco, consume alcohol, or caffeinated drinks.

Place an active heating blanket on the casualty’s anterior torso and under the arms in the axillae (to prevent burns, do not place any active heating source directly on the skin or wrap around the torso).

Because life signs at these temperatures are almost impossible to obtain, no one should be pronounced dead until he or she has been rewarmed; hence the use of the adage, “nobody is dead until warm and dead”.

conflict: (1) Adding external heat in the field: TB MED 508 (2026) says active external rewarming (hot water bottles, heated blankets and so on) 'should be applied only to individuals who have ceased shivering'; HHS Ship's Medicine Chest (2003) says that for moderate or severe hypothermia (not shivering, reduced consciousness or unconscious) 'External sources of heat should be used to rewarm the patient', with the skin insulated from warm objects, though it also calls aggressive rewarming of such patients 'usually ill-advised' outside hospital unless transport to definitive care is impossible; ATP 4-02.11 (2026) says 'Attempting to rewarm a severely hypothermic person should be done by medical professionals' and to focus on preventing further heat loss while waiting. The card shows the three positions; the owner must choose. Related: the JTS Hypothermia CPG (2023, written for trauma casualties) says to add external heat when possible; TC 21-3 (2025) puts a hot water bottle on the chest inside a hypothermia wrap for moderate hypothermia; ATP 3-50.21 (2018) says 'Begin to warm the body evenly and immediately' and suggests bare skin-on-skin contact in a sleeping bag for severe cases. (2) Hot water: HHS says no hot shower or hot bath for a person who is not shivering or not fully conscious (shown as an HHS warning) but allows one for mild hypothermia (alert and vigorously shivering); TB MED 508 lists 'warm water immersion' among the active techniques reserved for people who have ceased shivering. (3) Drinks: ATP 4-02.11 says 'If the casualty is conscious' and TB MED 508 says conscious or responsive patients, 'with supervision'; HHS is stricter: only patients 'fully conscious and who can eat or drink', and no food or fluids by mouth for those not shivering, with reduced consciousness or unconscious. The card uses the stricter HHS rule. (4) Exercise: TC 21-3 says 'Exercise mildly hypothermic patients'; TB MED 508 says exercise could cause an afterdrop and should be used only in stable patients; HHS says activity increases afterdrop and conscious patients should not be made to walk; ATP 4-02.11 says 'Avoid unnecessary movement from the casualty'. The card says to avoid unnecessary movement and does not recommend exercise. (5) Not breathing: TC 21-3 says to give rescue breathing for 3 to 15 minutes before moving a severely hypothermic casualty; TB MED 508 says to look for a pulse for at least 1 minute and start chest compressions if none is found; HHS says to check the pulse for 60 seconds. The card follows TB MED 508. FEMA P-2064 (2020) was searched: it only says to watch for signs of hypothermia.

review.notes: Re-review of the revised card (full check). Fixed: A6 drinks and sugary food only if 'fully alert and able to swallow' (HHS), W1 nothing by mouth if not shivering, drowsy, confused or unconscious (HHS), W2 no hot shower or bath and no sitting/standing/exercise for the not-shivering or not fully conscious (HHS), A8 lying flat (HHS), A10 now shows TB MED 508, HHS and ATP 4-02.11 positions on external heat, W4 cold skin easily burned (HHS, JTS). All other lines as confirmed in batch 1. No PDF junk. Recommended, not blocking: A10's HHS sentence ('external heat should be used for people who are not shivering...') drops HHS's condition: it calls aggressive rewarming of moderate/severe hypothermia 'usually ill-advised' outside hospital and endorses it 'when transportation to a site of definitive care is impossible'. Add '(when getting to medical care is not possible)' to that sentence. Not blocking because TB MED 508 independently supports external heat for the same non-shivering group and the conflict field records the caveat.
